g: History; Cold War foreign policy and political violence
sum: Vincent Bevins investigates the 1965–66 mass killings in Indonesia, in which an estimated half a million to a million people accused of being communists were murdered with the knowledge and support of the United States. He traces how the methods and the name Jakarta became a template for anti-communist violence across Latin America and beyond, reshaping the developing world during the Cold War.
bg: Published in 2020 by a journalist who reported from Brazil and Indonesia for the Los Angeles Times and The Washington Post. Bevins interviewed survivors and perpetrators in a dozen countries and drew on declassified American documents. It won wide praise and was translated into many languages.
br: Some background on the Cold War helps but is not essential; Bevins explains as he goes. The opening chapters on Indonesia’s independence and Sukarno set up the events of 1965.
la: Bevins combines investigative journalism with the personal stories of survivors, following a handful of individuals across decades so that the geopolitical history never loses its human scale. His argument is explicit and carefully sourced.
cx: The Indonesian killings remain little known in the West and politically sensitive in Indonesia itself. The book connects them to coups and repression in Brazil, Chile, Guatemala and elsewhere.
th: Hidden history
Some of the twentieth century’s largest massacres remain barely known.
Cold War violence
Anti-communism justified mass killing across the developing world.
The global South
The Cold War looked very different from Jakarta or São Paulo.
fit: Broadens your history shelf beyond the United States and Europe and pairs with How to Hide an Empire.
mis: Grim and relentless in places, and its argument about American responsibility will not suit every reader.
rq: Why are the Indonesian killings so little known?
How did the Jakarta method spread?
Which survivor’s story stayed with you?
dq: What responsibility does a country bear for violence it encourages abroad?
How does this change your view of the Cold War?
rel: Another hidden history of American power.

sum: C. L. R. James tells the story of the Haitian Revolution of 1791–1804, in which enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain, and founded the independent nation of Haiti. At its centre is Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man who became one of the great political and military leaders of his age.
bg: First published in 1938 and revised in 1963 with a new appendix, The Black Jacobins was written by a Trinidadian historian, novelist, cricket writer and Marxist thinker living in London. It became a foundational work of Caribbean, anti-colonial and Black radical history.
br: Some knowledge of the French Revolution helps, since events in Paris and Saint-Domingue constantly shape each other. Read the preface first; James explains his aims clearly. A map of Hispaniola is useful.
la: James writes vivid, dramatic narrative history, combining Marxist analysis of class and economy with a deep admiration for Toussaint as a tragic hero, whose flaws he analyses as carefully as his genius.
cx: Written as Africa and the Caribbean were moving toward independence from European empires, the book was intended partly as an inspiration and warning for anti-colonial movements of the 1930s and after.
th: Revolution and freedom
Enslaved people liberated themselves and defeated three European empires.
Leadership and tragedy
Toussaint’s genius and his fatal misjudgments are intertwined.
Empire and capitalism
Colonial wealth was built on the brutal economy of plantation slavery.
fit: A classic of history that complements The 1619 Project and The Wretched of the Earth on your list.
mis: Dense with names and events, and its Marxist framing and dramatic style may feel dated to some readers.
rq: What made Toussaint such a remarkable leader?
How did the French Revolution affect Saint-Domingue?
Where does James see Toussaint going wrong?
dq: Why is the Haitian Revolution less well known than the American or French revolutions?
What does the book suggest about leadership and the people?

sum: Frantz Fanon analyses colonialism as a system of violence that shapes both colonised and coloniser, argues that decolonisation is inevitably a violent struggle, and warns that newly independent nations risk being captured by a national middle class that simply replaces the colonisers. The book ends with case notes on the psychological wounds of colonial war.
bg: Fanon, a psychiatrist from Martinique who joined the Algerian independence movement, wrote the book in 1961 while dying of leukaemia; it was published with a famous preface by Jean-Paul Sartre shortly before his death at thirty-six. Its French title is Les Damnés de la Terre.
br: The opening chapter on violence is the most famous and controversial; read the whole book to see how Fanon’s concerns broaden to national culture, class and mental health.
la: Fanon writes with urgency and fury, combining political analysis, psychiatry and revolutionary manifesto; his prose moves between clinical precision and passionate rhetoric. Even readers who reject his conclusions often find his diagnosis of colonial psychology hard to forget, and his clinical eye sharpens every chapter.
cx: Written during the brutal Algerian War of Independence (1954–1962), the book became a key text for anti-colonial and Black liberation movements worldwide, including the Black Panthers.
th: Colonial violence
Colonialism is founded on violence and shapes everyone it touches.
National consciousness
Independence can fail if a new elite replaces the old.
Psychological wounds
Colonial war leaves deep mental scars on everyone involved.
fit: Pairs with The Black Jacobins and the existentialists on your list, especially Sartre.
mis: Its defence of revolutionary violence is deeply controversial, and the prose can be dense.
cw: Psychiatric case studies of war trauma.
rq: How does Fanon define colonial violence?
What does he fear about national elites?
What do the case notes add to the argument?
dq: Is Fanon’s view of violence justified?
How do his warnings apply to post-colonial nations today?

sum: James Baldwin’s two essays address America’s racial crisis. The first is a letter to his fourteen-year-old nephew on the centenary of emancipation. The second recounts his own adolescent religious awakening, his break with the church, and his encounter with the Nation of Islam’s Elijah Muhammad, before calling on Black and white Americans to end the racial nightmare together.
bg: Published in 1963, at the height of the civil rights movement, the book became a bestseller and made Baldwin a national figure. The second essay first appeared in The New Yorker in 1962 under the title Letter from a Region in My Mind.
br: Short: read it in one or two sittings and then reread passages. Baldwin’s sentences are long, rhythmic and best read slowly, almost aloud. The first essay is only a few pages long.
la: Baldwin writes with prophetic intensity, combining memoir, sermon and argument; his style draws on the King James Bible and the Black church even as he criticises them. He addresses readers intimately, as if speaking across a table.
cx: Written months before the March on Washington, it captures the moral urgency of the early 1960s and remains a touchstone for writing about race in America.
th: Love and responsibility
Baldwin calls for love as a demanding, transformative force.
Religion and power
Churches can liberate and oppress at the same time.
Facing history
America must confront its past to have any future.
fit: Pairs with The Souls of Black Folk and The New Jim Crow on your list.
mis: Its religious and rhetorical intensity may not suit every reader, and its argument is more prophetic than programmatic.
rq: What does Baldwin want his nephew to understand?
Why does he leave the church?
What does he make of Elijah Muhammad?
dq: Is love a political force for Baldwin?
How has America answered his challenge?

sum: W. E. B. Du Bois’s collection of essays examines Black life in America after emancipation. It introduces the ideas of the veil and double consciousness, the sense of always looking at oneself through others’ eyes, criticises Booker T. Washington’s accommodationism, and moves from history and sociology to memoir, a short story and a meditation on the spirituals, the sorrow songs.
bg: Published in 1903, the book is a landmark of African American literature and sociology. Du Bois was the first Black American to earn a Harvard doctorate and later co-founded the NAACP. He lived to ninety-five and died in Ghana in 1963, on the eve of the March on Washington.
br: Each chapter opens with lines of poetry and a few bars of a spiritual; the essays vary in style, so take them one at a time. The chapter on the death of his son is among the most moving.
la: Du Bois combines scholarly analysis, lyrical prose and personal narrative, deliberately moving between registers to capture the complexity of Black experience. The book’s structure, with music and poetry framing each chapter, makes an argument about Black culture’s richness that the prose then confirms.
cx: Written in the era of Jim Crow segregation and lynching, the book influenced the civil rights movement and remains foundational to debates on race and identity.
th: Double consciousness
Black Americans see themselves through the eyes of a hostile world.
The veil
A barrier, often invisible to white Americans, separates Black and white America.
Education and progress
Du Bois argues for higher education against Washington’s narrower vocational path.
fit: A foundation for the race and history titles on your list, and a natural companion to Baldwin.
mis: The variety of styles can feel uneven, and some historical references need context.
cw: Grief over the death of a child.
rq: What does double consciousness mean to you?
Why does Du Bois disagree with Washington?
How do the sorrow songs frame the book?
dq: Is the color line still the problem of this century?
How does Du Bois’s style serve his argument?
